title: Magna Carta
objective: After this level you can explain what Magna Carta said in 1215 and why it still matters.
summary: In June 1215 rebel barons forced King John to accept Magna Carta. The Pope annulled it within ten weeks, but it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three clauses are still law.

cards.headline: In June 1215 a king agreed to a charter. By August, the Pope had killed it.
cards.body: Magna Carta, the “Great Charter”, was dead in less than ten weeks. So why does anyone still care about it? Because it refused to stay dead.

cards.headline: Peace terms in a meadow
cards.body: By 1215 England’s barons had had enough of King John. The rebels renounced their allegiance and occupied London. On 15 June, at Runnymede, a meadow between Windsor and Staines, John agreed to their charter. Its most famous promise, clause 39: no free man could be imprisoned or stripped of his rights except by the lawful judgment of his equals or the law of the land. Clause 40 added that the king would not sell, deny or delay justice to anyone. In short: the king can’t just lock you up.

cards.headline: Dead in ten weeks
cards.body: It didn’t last. John had submitted his kingdom to the Pope, so he appealed to him. On 24 August 1215, less than ten weeks after Runnymede, Pope Innocent III annulled the charter, calling it “shameful, demeaning, illegal and unjust”. Fighting broke out again in September and went on until John died in October 1216. As peace deals go, it was a flop.

mascot.line: Hold on to this flop. The next levels show why the charter didn’t stay dead.

cards.headline: The charter that kept coming back
cards.body: Then something odd happened. After John’s death the charter was reissued in the name of his young son, Henry III, in 1216 and again in 1217. In 1225 it came back once more, this time in exchange for a new tax. The failed peace deal had become a bargain: rights for money. And pieces of it are still here. Three clauses remain in English law today: the freedom of the English Church, the ancient liberties of the City of London, and the right to lawful judgment.
cards.callout: Three clauses of Magna Carta are still English law

cards.headline: Magna Carta: known
learned: King John agreed to it at Runnymede in June 1215
Clause 39: no imprisonment without lawful judgment
The Pope annulled it within ten weeks
Reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225; three clauses are still law

questions.prompt: What did Magna Carta’s clause 39 promise a free man in 1215?

options.label: That he could never be taxed by the king without a vote
options.rationale: Taxes came into the story later, in 1225.

options.label: That he could vote for members of the king’s council
No imprisonment without lawful judgment or the law of the land
That the Church, not the king, would judge all his crimes
options.rationale: Clause 39 is about lawful judgment, not church courts.

questions.explanation: Clause 39: no free man imprisoned or stripped of his rights except by the lawful judgment of his equals or the law of the land.

questions.prompt: Pope Innocent III annulled Magna Carta in 1215. Why didn’t that finish it off?

options.label: King John ignored the Pope and obeyed it
options.rationale: John was the one who asked the Pope to annul it.

options.label: The barons had already carved it in stone
options.rationale: It survived on parchment, by being reissued.

options.label: The Pope changed his mind a week later
options.rationale: The annulment stood; the charter came back by reissue.

questions.explanation: After John’s death it was reissued for Henry III in 1216 and 1217, and again in 1225 in exchange for a new tax.

questions.prompt: Level 5’s Justinian had Roman law sorted on an emperor’s orders. How did Magna Carta come about differently?

options.label: A church council wrote it for the Pope
options.rationale: The Pope annulled it; he didn’t write it.

options.label: A commission of lawyers compiled old laws
The king wrote it to reward loyal towns
Rebel barons forced it on their king

questions.explanation: Justinian’s code came from the top; Magna Carta was forced on King John by rebel barons who had occupied London.
